title: Impulsive to foolhardy: acting before thinking
core: All three describe action that outruns judgment — the deed happens before deliberation catches up. They share a mild-to-strong disapproval that is aimed at the *absence of thought*, not at bad intent; nobody described this way is malicious, only unbraked. What separates them is what fills the gap where thought should have been: nothing at all, heat, or nerve. They also differ in whether they label a person's standing habit or a single spectacular decision.

words.nuance: The only one where risk never entered the picture — there is no danger being defied, just no pause. It labels a **temperament** you'd describe over years rather than one decision, which is why it can be said fondly about a friend.

The gap is filled by **feeling** — anger, love, pride — so it carries heat and forward motion. It attaches to a single headlong act with a whiff of romance (an impetuous proposal, an impetuous resignation), and leaves the reader half-impressed by the fire.

The only one that requires **visible danger** and real nerve spent on it. The actor saw the drop and jumped anyway, so the word is a verdict on the odds — it implies this will end badly, where the other two only imply it was unconsidered.

exam_note: All three fit "acted without thinking," so the sentence must name the discriminator: an emotion word points to impetuous, a stated hazard or feat of nerve to foolhardy, and a bare description of character to impulsive.
